items.stem: Which of the following statements about mechanical waves is correct?
items.answer: y = A sin(kx − ωt) represents a wave moving in the +x direction.
items.markingKey: (b) Correct: "y = A sin(kx − ωt) represents a wave moving in the +x direction." The other three are false.
options: Sound waves in air are transverse.
y = A sin(kx − ωt) represents a wave moving in the +x direction.
y = A sin(kx + ωt) represents a wave moving in the +x direction.
A wave carries the particles of the medium along with it.

items.stem: Why can transverse mechanical waves not travel through gases?
items.answer: Gases have no shear rigidity, so they cannot transmit a sideways restoring force.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Sound cannot travel through a vacuum.
Reason (R): Sound is a mechanical wave that needs a material medium.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: A sound wave of frequency 1000 Hz travels in air at 330 m s⁻¹. Find its wavelength.
A wave on a string is described by y(x, t) = 2 sin(1x − 10t), with x and y in cm and t in seconds. Find the amplitude, wavelength, period, speed and direction of propagation.
items.answer: A = 2 cm, λ = 6.28 cm, T = 0.628 s, v = 10.0 cm s⁻¹, along +x
items.markingKey: Compare with y = A sin(kx ∓ ωt): λ = 2π/k = 6.28 cm; T = 2π/ω = 0.628 s; v = ω/k = 10.0 cm s⁻¹; the minus sign means travel along +x.

items.markingKey: (c) String elements move perpendicular to the wave.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the wave velocity and the particle velocity for a wave on a string.
items.answer: Wave velocity v = ω/k is the speed of the disturbance; particle velocity ∂y/∂t is the speed of each element moving up and down and varies with time.

items.markingKey: Compare with y = A sin(kx ∓ ωt): λ = 2π/k = 6.28 m; T = 2π/ω = 1.26 s; v = ω/k = 5.00 m s⁻¹; the plus sign means travel along −x.

items.answer: At constant temperature, the speed of sound in a gas does not depend on pressure.

options: Newton's formula for the speed of sound in air gives the correct value.

The speed of sound in air increases with pressure at constant temperature.

items.stem: Why is the speed of sound in a gas independent of pressure at constant temperature?
items.answer: P/ρ = RT/M is constant at fixed T, so √(γP/ρ) does not change.

items.stem:

items.stem: A string of linear mass density 2 g m⁻¹ is stretched with a tension of 20 N. Find the speed of transverse waves on it.

Tara claps near a cliff and hears the echo 0.5 s later. If the speed of sound is 330 m s⁻¹, how far away is the cliff?
items.markingKey: Sound goes to the cliff and back: 2d = vt ⇒ d = 330 × 0.5/2 = 82.5 m.

items.stem: A string of linear mass density 1 g m⁻¹ is stretched with a tension of 80 N. Find the speed of transverse waves on it.
What was wrong with Newton's formula for the speed of sound in air, and how did Laplace correct it?
items.answer: Newton assumed isothermal changes (v = √(P/ρ) ≈ 280 m s⁻¹); Laplace said they are adiabatic, v = √(γP/ρ) ≈ 331 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Why does sound travel faster on a hot day?
items.answer: v ∝ √T for a gas; higher temperature gives a higher speed.

items.stem: Why is there a phase change of π when a wave on a string is reflected from a rigid support?
items.answer: The support cannot move, so the displacement there must stay zero; the reflected wave must be inverted to cancel the incident wave at that point.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Energy is not transported along a standing wave.
Reason (R): Nodes never move.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (b) Both true; R alone is not the full reason (equal and opposite energy flows cancel).
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: A standing wave of frequency 120 Hz is set up on a string in which waves travel at 80 m s⁻¹. Find the distance between two adjacent nodes.

A standing wave on a string is given by y = 0.04 sin(πx) cos(50πt) (x, y in m, t in s). Find (i) the wavelength, (ii) the frequency, (iii) the speed of the component waves and (iv) the positions of the first three nodes from x = 0.
items.markingKey: (i) λ = 2π/k (1). (ii) ν = ω/2π (1). (iii) v = ω/k (1). (iv) nodes where sin kx = 0: x = nλ/2 (1). Each component wave has amplitude 0.02 m.

items.stem: Two waves of the same frequency with amplitudes 2 mm and 2 mm superpose at a point with a phase difference of 180°. Find the amplitude of the resultant.
Two identical waves of amplitude 2 mm and wavelength 0.4 m travel in opposite directions on a string with a node at x = 0. Find the amplitude of vibration at x = 0.15 m.
items.markingKey: y = 2A sin(kx) cos ωt (1); amplitude = 2A|sin(2πx/λ)| = 4 × |sin(135°)| (1) = 2.83 mm (1).

items.stem: A string fixed at both ends, 100 cm long, has two successive resonant frequencies of 375 Hz and 450 Hz, and no resonance between them. Find (i) the fundamental frequency, (ii) which harmonics these are and (iii) the speed of waves on the string.
items.answer: (i) 75 Hz (ii) the 5th and 6th harmonics (iii) 150 m s⁻¹
items.markingKey: (i) successive harmonics differ by the fundamental: 450 − 375 = 75 Hz (2). (ii) 375/75 = 5 (1). (iii) ν₁ = v/2L ⇒ v = 2Lν₁ = 150 m s⁻¹ (2).

items.stem: How is a standing wave formed on a string fixed at both ends?
items.answer: Waves travelling in opposite directions (incident and reflected) with the same amplitude and frequency superpose to give fixed nodes and antinodes.

items.stem: Two waves of the same frequency with amplitudes 3 mm and 4 mm superpose at a point with a phase difference of 0°. Find the amplitude of the resultant.
Which of the following statements about standing waves is correct?
items.answer: At a rigid boundary a reflected wave undergoes a phase change of π.
items.markingKey: (c) Correct: "At a rigid boundary a reflected wave undergoes a phase change of π." The other three are false.
options: The distance between two adjacent nodes is λ.
All points of a standing wave vibrate with the same amplitude.
At a rigid boundary a reflected wave undergoes a phase change of π.
At an open boundary the reflected wave undergoes a phase change of π.

items.stem: A standing wave of frequency 100 Hz is set up on a string in which waves travel at 40 m s⁻¹. Find the distance between two adjacent nodes.
items.markingKey: λ = v/ν = 40/100 = 0.4 m; node-to-node = λ/2 = 20.0 cm.

items.stem: Derive the normal-mode frequencies of a string of length L fixed at both ends.
items.markingKey: Nodes at both ends ⇒ L = nλ/2 (3); ν = v/λ (2).

items.stem: A string fixed at both ends, 80 cm long, has two successive resonant frequencies of 120 Hz and 160 Hz, and no resonance between them. Find (i) the fundamental frequency, (ii) which harmonics these are and (iii) the speed of waves on the string.
items.answer: (i) 40 Hz (ii) the 3rd and 4th harmonics (iii) 64 m s⁻¹
items.markingKey: (i) successive harmonics differ by the fundamental: 160 − 120 = 40 Hz (2). (ii) 120/40 = 3 (1). (iii) ν₁ = v/2L ⇒ v = 2Lν₁ = 64 m s⁻¹ (2).

items.stem: Show that the superposition of y₁ = a sin(kx − ωt) and y₂ = a sin(kx + ωt) gives a standing wave, and find the positions of nodes and antinodes.
items.answer: y = 2a sin kx cos ωt; nodes at x = nλ/2, antinodes at x = (n + ½)λ/2
items.markingKey: Add using sin C + sin D (2); amplitude 2a sin kx (1); nodes sin kx = 0 (1); antinodes |sin kx| = 1 (1).

items.stem: A standing wave on a string is given by y = 0.2 sin(π/4x) cos(50πt) (x, y in m, t in s). Find (i) the wavelength, (ii) the frequency, (iii) the speed of the component waves and (iv) the positions of the first three nodes from x = 0.
items.markingKey: (i) λ = 2π/k (1). (ii) ν = ω/2π (1). (iii) v = ω/k (1). (iv) nodes where sin kx = 0: x = nλ/2 (1). Each component wave has amplitude 0.1 m.

items.stem: Two identical waves of amplitude 6 mm and wavelength 2 m travel in opposite directions on a string with a node at x = 0. Find the amplitude of vibration at x = 0.1667 m.
items.markingKey: y = 2A sin(kx) cos ωt (1); amplitude = 2A|sin(2πx/λ)| = 12 × |sin(30°)| (1) = 6.00 mm (1).

items.answer: (i) 141 m s⁻¹ (ii) 88.4 Hz (iii) it doubles (iv) the vibrating length becomes shorter, so ν = v/2L increases

items.stem: A tuning fork of unknown frequency gives 5 beats per second with a standard fork of 288 Hz. When the unknown fork is loaded with a little wax, the number of beats decreases. What is its frequency?

items.stem: Why does the pitch of the sound rise as a bottle is filled with water?

items.stem: In a resonance-column experiment, Ishita uses a tuning fork of 480 Hz and finds the first two resonance lengths of the air column as 16.5 cm and 51.5 cm. Find the speed of sound in air and the end correction.

items.stem: In a resonance-column experiment, Aditi uses a tuning fork of 512 Hz and finds the first two resonance lengths of the air column as 15.8 cm and 49.5 cm. Find the speed of sound in air and the end correction.
